So the Greeks had a different way that they could deduce the size of the moon. Next time you see a full moon rising, try to measure how long it takes.
cues.zh: 阿里斯塔克斯就这么做过。他测出地月距离大约是 60 个地球半径。实际上，这个轨道在 58 到 62 之间变动。所以这结果已经相当准了。准得不能再准了。没错。我之前提到过，通过月食可以观察到月球和地球的相对大小。月球的直径大约是地球的四分之一。但在实际操作中，没有摄影技术很难做到精确测量。所以古希腊人用了另一种方法来推算月球的大小。下次看到满月升起时，不妨试着测一下它升起花了多久。

cues.en: What you should find is that it's around two minutes.
cues.zh: 你该会发现，大约是两分钟。

cues.en: What you're watching is not so much the moon moving through the orbit. Instead, it's that as you and the Earth are rotating, your line of sight over the horizon is scanning over the moon. The moon basically takes twenty four hours to to cycle around the Earth, at least as observed by us because of the Earth's rotation. Actually, slightly less because the moon's also moving, but basically twenty four hours. And so therefore, you can work out the ratio between the radius of the moon and the distance to the moon, just by taking the ratio between two minutes and twenty four hours. So because they knew the distance to the moon, they could use this to figure out the radius.
cues.zh: 你看到的其实并不是月球在轨道上移动。而是当你和地球一起自转时，你越过地平线的视线正在扫过月球。基本上，月球绕地球一圈需要二十四小时，至少在我们看来如此，因为地球在自转。实际上略短一些，因为月球也在移动，但基本上是二十四小时。因此，你可以通过取两分钟与二十四小时之比，算出月球半径与到月球距离之比。所以，既然他们知道到月球的距离，就能用这个算出月球的半径。

cues.en: Now keep in mind, both of their estimates could be at best approximately true. Since the real orbit of the moon is an ellipse, it's not a perfect circle. But the point is that with almost no technology, they had pretty decent estimates for the size of the moon and how far away it was.
cues.zh: 记住，他们两人的估算充其量只是近似正确。因为月球的真实轨道是椭圆，而不是完美的圆。但关键在于，几乎没有什么技术，他们就能对月球的大小和距离做出相当不错的估算。

cues.en: The sun was trickier. So at the time, they they thought the sun went around the earth, but it actually it actually doesn't matter for the argument whether the sun goes around the earth or earth goes around the sun. Well, again, there's these two numbers. There's the size of the sun and the distance of the sun. Mhmm. You can compute the ratio again, because of eclipses. And this is weird coincidence.
cues.zh: 太阳就更棘手了。当时，他们认为太阳绕着地球转，但其实太阳绕地球转还是地球绕太阳转，对这个论证并不重要。同样，还是这两个数字：太阳的大小和太阳的距离。嗯。由于日食，你可以再次计算出比值。这真是个奇怪的巧合。

cues.en: I mean, there's no reason why it should be true. But when there's a solar eclipse, the moon and the sun are almost exactly the same size. Yeah. I guess it's not true for lunar eclipses. Lunar eclipses, as we saw, the Earth's shadow is much bigger.
cues.zh: 我觉得这没有什么必然道理。但日食时，月亮和太阳看起来几乎一样大。是啊，我想月食就不是这样了。正如我们看到的，月食时地球的影子要大得多。

cues.en: But for some reason, they are almost the same size. What this means is that if you look at the ratio between the radius of the moon and the distance that it is away from the Earth, which is what determines how big it looks to us up in the sky,
cues.zh: 但不知为何，它们看起来几乎一样大。这意味着，如果你看月亮的半径与它到地球的距离之比，这个比例决定了它在天空中看起来有多大，

cues.en: because of this solar eclipse coincidence, that has to be the same as the ratio between the radius of the sun and its distance away from the Earth.
cues.zh: 由于日食时的这种巧合，这个比例必须和太阳的半径与它到地球的距离之比相同。

cues.en: As we saw, the Greeks already knew that ratio for the moon. The point is that they could get at least an approximate sense for the size of the sun if they could figure out how far away it is or vice versa. Now the animation I'm showing right now is very grossly not to scale. You and I both know that the sun is actually much, much farther away than the moon is. But, of course, that's not obvious when you just look at it in the sky, and so you might wonder, how could you conclude that it has to be so far away? In ancient times, for all people knew, seeing that it was roughly the same size as the moon in the sky, it could be, say, twice as far away as the moon is and only twice as big. In fact, for the animation, I'm gonna go ahead and leave it unrealistically close like this because it helps clarify how the next logical step works. How do you work out the distance to the sun? You can use the moon. That's almost the only available object you can use. But, you do something else. You look at phases of the moon.
cues.zh: 正如我们所见，古希腊人已经知道了月球的这一比例。关键在于，只要能算出太阳有多远，他们就能大致估算出太阳的大小，反之亦然。不过，我现在展示的动画严重不成比例。你我都知道，太阳实际上比月球要遥远得多。但是，仅凭肉眼仰望天空，这一点显然并不直观，所以你可能会好奇，怎么就能断定它一定有那么远呢？在古代，人们只看到太阳和月亮在天空中大小相仿，完全可能认为太阳只是比月球远一倍，体积大一倍而已。事实上，在动画里我会继续保留这种极不真实的近距离，因为这有助于讲清接下来的逻辑步骤。那么，该如何测算到太阳的距离呢？你可以利用月球。这几乎是唯一可用的天体了。不过，你得另辟蹊径。你要观察月相。

cues.en: The sun illuminates
cues.zh: 太阳照亮了

cues.en: half of the the moon. And so we on Earth,
cues.zh: 月亮的一半。所以地球上的我们

cues.en: we also see half the moon, but it's a different half. And so because of that, we get phases of the moon.
cues.zh: 看到的也是月亮的一半，但不是同一半。因此，月亮才会有盈亏变化。

cues.en: This is also, by the way, why we know the moon is round.
cues.zh: 顺便说一句，这也是我们知道月亮是圆的原因。

cues.en: If the moon was flat, we would not get phases. We would get either a dim moon or a lit moon, but we wouldn't get these phases.
cues.zh: 如果月亮是平的，就不会有盈亏变化。我们看到的只会是暗月或亮月，不会有这些变化。

cues.en: Sometimes you get a full moon. If the moon is over here, you you see the whole lit thing. Sometimes you get a new moon over here, and sometimes you you get a half moon. You can pretty much rediscover for yourself a way to estimate the distance to the sun by asking when exactly a half moon occurs.
cues.zh: 有时会出现满月。月亮在这里时，你能看到整个月面都被照亮。有时这里会出现新月，有时会出现半月。你几乎可以自己重新推算出一种估算太阳距离的方法：只要问问半月究竟什么时候出现。

cues.en: From the name, you would guess that it's halfway between a new moon and a full moon, but that's actually not true. Half moon occurs not when the moon and the sun make a right angle at the earth, but actually when the earth and the sun make a right angle at the moon. Hopefully, your graph would be better than the one I'm drawing here. Okay. Hopefully, this makes some sense. For us to see a half moon, it means that the side of the moon that we see facing us overlaps by exactly 90 degrees with the side of the moon being illuminated by the sun, which in turn means we have a right angle at the spot labeled here.
cues.zh: 从名字上猜，你会以为它在新月和满月之间，但其实不是这样。半月出现的时候，并不是月亮和太阳在地球处成直角，而是地球和太阳在月亮处成直角。希望你们画的图比我这里画的好。好了，希望这能说得通。我们要看到半月，意味着我们看到的朝向我们的那半个月球，正好和太阳照亮的那半个月球重叠90度，这也就意味着，在标注的这个位置有一个直角。

cues.en: As as your lovely illustration will show, half moons are slightly closer to new moons than they are to full moon... From moons. Of course, in this graphic, the effect is very exaggerated because the sun is being drawn so close to the Earth. How far away the sun is determines when exactly that half moon occurs.
cues.zh: 正如这幅精美的插图所示，半月比起满月，和新月更接近一些……说的是月相。当然，这张图里这种效果被夸大了，因为太阳画得离地球很近。太阳离得有多远，决定了半月具体会在什么时候出现。

cues.en: The farther away, the closer it is to the true halfway point. In fact, you can make this a little more quantitative
cues.zh: 太阳离得越远，半月就越接近真正的中间点。事实上，我们可以稍微定量地描述一下：

cues.en: where if you measure the angle separating that halfway point between new moons and full moons from the point of a half moon, which again is confusingly not the same thing, then intuitively you can see how a smaller angle means a larger distance to the sun.
cues.zh: 测量新月和满月之间的中间点与半月位置之间的夹角——这里说的半月，容易让人混淆，其实指的不是同一个点。直观上，夹角越小，太阳就离得越远。

cues.en: And more precisely, when you do the little bit of trigonometry here, you can conclude that the distance to the sun is the same as the distance to the moon divided by the sine of that angle. This is where the Greeks started hitting a wall of technology. What they did is that they knew that the moon took twenty eight days to go around the Earth, and so they had to measure exactly when a half moon occurred and what the deviation is. Now, Aristarchus, he thought that the the the distance was six hours. Half moons occurred six hours before the midpoint between new moon and the moon. He doesn't write how he came up with this. And
cues.zh: 更准确地说，只要用一点三角学知识，就能得出日地距离等于月地距离除以那个角的正弦值。古希腊人就是在这里撞上了技术瓶颈。他们的做法是，已知月球绕地球一圈需要 28 天，所以他们必须精确测量半月出现的时刻以及其中的偏差。而阿里斯塔克斯当时认为这个时间差是 6 小时。半月出现在新月和满月中点前的 6 个小时。他没有写明自己是怎么得出这个结论的。而且

cues.en: it's wrong. The the actual discrepancy is half an hour. He's off by a huge factor. So the thing is,
cues.zh: 这是错的。实际的时间偏差只有半小时。他的误差大得离谱。所以问题在于，

cues.en: well, we have clocks, which work in the dark. They had sundials and... Which don't work in the dark. They also did not have telescopes. Mathematically,
cues.zh: 我们有能在黑暗中走的钟表，而他们用日晷……在黑暗中根本没法用，而且他们也没有望远镜。从数学上讲，

cues.en: their method was sound. Technologically, it was just not possible for this method to work. No. But it worked well enough. Okay. So he was off by basically a whole order of magnitude. He thought that the sun was 20 times further away than the moon. The true answer, based on the slight change to that angle that he was trying to measure, is more like 370
cues.zh: 他们的方法是可行的。但受限于技术，这种方法根本不可能成功。确实，但已经算很管用了。好吧，他的误差基本差了一个数量级。他以为太阳到地球的距离是月球的 20 倍，而根据他试图测量的那个微小角度变化，真实答案其实大约是 370

cues.en: times the distance to the moon. And he thought that the sun was seven times bigger than the Earth, when in fact it is, a 109 times bigger. Even with that
cues.zh: 倍。他还以为太阳是地球的 7 倍大，而实际上是 109 倍大。尽管有这样

cues.en: lousy
cues.zh: 糟糕的

cues.en: measurement,
cues.zh: 测量数据，

cues.en: Aristarchus
cues.zh: Aristarchus

cues.en: was the first to make a really important conclusion, which is that the sun did not revolve around the earth. The sun was seven times... Well, he thought the sun was seven times larger. Why would the sun go around the earth? So the earth should go around the sun.
cues.zh: 却第一个得出了一个至关重要的结论：太阳并不绕着地球转。太阳比地球大 7 倍……好吧，他以为太阳大 7 倍。既然如此，太阳凭什么绕着地球转呢？所以应该是地球绕着太阳转。

cues.en: Qualitatively, conclusion was correct. It's just that the sun is much, much larger than he thought. But he was the first. And like, it's not obvious, you know, you look at the sun, know, it's this big. Really. Okay. But it's actually a 100 times bigger than the earth. So he was the first to propose the heliocentric model, actually. If you look at Copernicus'
cues.zh: 定性上看，结论是对的。只不过太阳比他以为的大得多得多。但他是第一人。而且这并不显然，你知道，你看着太阳，觉得它就那么大。真的。但它其实比地球大100倍。所以他其实是第一个提出日心说的人。如果你看哥白尼的

cues.en: famous book, he says, you know, Aristarchus proposed the heliocentric model. And the other Greeks
cues.zh: 那本名著，他说，你知道，阿利斯塔克提出了日心说。而其他希腊人

cues.en: dismissed him for good mathematical reasons, but again they were limited by the technology. They said that it doesn't make sense for the Earth to grow around the sun because if the Earth were growing on the sun, the position of the shape of the constellations would shift as you go from one side of sun to the other, and we don't see that. This is an important point to emphasize because it's gonna come up again for us later when we figure out the size of the galaxy.
cues.zh: 以充分的数学理由驳回了它，但同样，他们受限于技术。他们说，地球绕太阳转说不通，因为如果地球绕太阳转，那么从太阳的一侧到另一侧，星座的形状和位置就会发生偏移，而我们并没有观察到这一点。这一点很重要，值得强调，因为后面我们测算星系大小时还会再遇到它。

cues.en: So if you've got a bunch of stars sitting here in three-dimensional space and you picture yourself as an observer staring at those stars and you move around through that three-dimensional space,
cues.zh: 假设这里有一群恒星，分布在三维空间中。你可以想象自己是观察者，望着这些恒星，在三维空间里移动。

cues.en: then the apparent relative position of those stars shifts around as you move. We call this parallax. It's the same phenomenon where if you're on a car in the highway and you look out, all of the nearby trees seem to be moving much more quickly than the background mountains.
cues.zh: 随着你的移动，这些恒星看起来彼此之间的位置也会发生变化。我们把这种现象叫作视差。就像你坐在高速公路上的车里向外看，附近的树看起来比远处的山移动得快得多。

cues.en: So when Aristarchus says, hey, guys, maybe the earth is going around the sun,
cues.zh: 所以当阿里斯塔克斯说：伙计们，也许地球是绕着太阳转的，

cues.en: all of his fellow Greeks are like, well, if that was true and you've got this earth sun system sitting among a bunch of stars,
cues.zh: 他的希腊同胞们就反驳道：好吧，如果真是这样，这套地日系统又置身于群星之中，

cues.en: then for us, the observers sitting here on the planet earth, as we move around through space from winter to spring to summer and it's going to be quite a bit of movement through space since evidently the sun is supposed to be quite far away from the earth then because of this parallax we should see a change in the pattern of the stars. The nearby stars should be moving a little bit more than the background stars, and the overall shape of the constellations should slowly drift through the seasons.
cues.zh: 那么对我们这些坐在地球上的观测者来说，随着我们在太空中从冬季穿行到春季再到夏季——而且由于太阳显然离地球相当远，这在太空中的位移会非常大——那么由于这种视差，我们理应看到星象格局发生变化：较近的恒星移动幅度应该比背景恒星稍大一些，而星座的整体形状也应该随着季节慢慢漂移。

cues.en: But that's not what we see. The constellations seem to be the same shape between the summer and the winter. And that would only be possible if the stars were much, much, much further away than we currently think they are. So, Aristarchus, if you were to accept your model, we must make the universe thousands and thousands times bigger. Therefore, we are not going to... We're going dismiss your theory. It shows you that that even when you have the math right, you don't necessarily get to the truth because, of course, the universe is in in fact in in fact not just thousands of times larger than the theory, but actually billions and trillions of times larger. This is not an obvious fact. At this point, let's jump ahead quite a bit in history up to Kepler,
cues.zh: 但这并不是我们观察到的。夏季和冬季的星座形状似乎是一样的。而只有当恒星比我们目前认为的要远得多得多时，这才可能成立。所以，阿里斯塔克斯，如果你要接受你的模型，我们就必须把宇宙放大成千上万倍。因此，我们不会……我们要驳回你的理论。这说明，即使你的数学是对的，你也不一定能得到真相，因为当然，宇宙实际上不仅比理论大几千倍，而是实际上大数十亿、数万亿倍。这并不是一个显而易见的事实。到这里，让我们在历史上向前跳一大步，来到开普勒，

cues.en: perhaps the best part of this whole story. This is the most genius step of the ladder. The first time you climb from one step to the next, it's always heroic. Because
cues.zh: 也许整个故事中最精彩的部分就在这里。这是阶梯上最天才的一步。你第一次从一级爬到下一级时，总是很英雄。因为

cues.en: the first time, you're at the edge of what the data and the math and the technology can give you. Now Kepler was not working from a blank slate. He was building off of the work of others, most notably that of Copernicus.
cues.zh: 第一次，你处在数据、数学和技术所能给你的极限边缘。开普勒并不是从零开始。他是在别人的工作基础上继续前进，尤其是哥白尼的工作。

cues.en: So Copernicus had already worked out that the planets move around the sun. He said that the planets move around the sun in circular orbits,
cues.zh: 哥白尼已经弄清楚了行星围绕太阳运动。他说行星以圆形轨道绕太阳运行，

cues.en: and he even figured out the period, how long it takes for each planet going on the sun. So for example, we know that the Earth takes exactly one year to do a full orbit, and Copernicus had figured out that Mars takes six hundred eighty seven days for its orbit and likewise for all the other known planets. He gets all the fame because of heliocentrism,
cues.zh: 他甚至算出了周期，也就是每颗行星绕太阳一圈需要多长时间。比如，我们知道地球完整绕一圈正好需要一年，而哥白尼已经算出火星轨道需要六百八十七天，其他已知行星也是如此。他因为日心说而获得了所有名声，

cues.en: but these numbers were arguably his most important contribution. You'll see in a moment why they are critical. The way he computed this was that he had all this Babylonian data. Essentially, the way this worked was by compiling centuries
cues.zh: 但可以说，这些数字才是他最重要的贡献。你马上就会看到它们为何如此关键。他的计算方法是利用这些巴比伦数据。简单来说，他把数百年来的观测资料汇总起来，找出规律。

cues.en: observations for where the planets appear among the stars,
cues.zh: 记录行星在星空中出现的位置，

cues.en: then figuring out when those patterns repeat, and then very importantly, factoring in the movement of Earth in that time.
cues.zh: 然后找出这些规律何时会再次出现。还有一点至关重要：要把这段时间里地球的运动也考虑进去。

cues.en: Kepler was interested in figuring out the relative sizes of all of these orbits.
cues.zh: 开普勒当时很想弄清所有这些轨道的相对大小。

cues.en: He had this funny little pet theory that was linked to the five platonic solids.
cues.zh: 他有个很有意思的独门理论，和五种柏拉图多面体有关。

cues.en: The idea was if you imagine a sphere inscribed in an octahedron,
cues.zh: 他的设想是：先想象一个内切于正八面体的球体，

cues.en: and then you fit the smallest possible sphere around that, and then fit the smallest possible icosahedron
cues.zh: 然后在外层套一个尽可能小的外接球体，再给它套上一个尽可能小的正二十面体，

cues.en: around that, then layer on another sphere and then a dodecahedron,
cues.zh: 接着再叠上一层球体，然后是一个正十二面体，

cues.en: one more sphere, then a tetrahedron,
cues.zh: 再加一个球体，接着是一个正四面体，

cues.en: one more sphere,
cues.zh: 又一个球体，

cues.en: a cube, and then one final sphere.
cues.zh: 一个正方体，最后再加上最后一个球体。

cues.en: You get these six spheres, and the ratios between the sizes of those spheres, Kepler believed, would match the ratios of the orbits for the six known planets.
cues.zh: 这样你会得到六个球体。开普勒认为，这些球体的大小比例，会与当时已知六颗行星的轨道比例相吻合。

cues.en: Since these are the platonic solids, it somehow feels like a very natural or universal set of ratios. It would have been a beautiful theory. This was true. So hungry to prove his very beautiful theory, he needed to look at the historical data for where all the planets appeared in the sky. There was this astronomer at the time, Tycho Brahe, who was this very wealthy eccentric,
cues.zh: 既然它们是柏拉图立体，这组比例不知为何让人觉得如此自然，仿佛放之四海而皆准。这本该是个优美的理论。事实也的确如此。为了证明这个优美的理论，他急切地需要查阅历史数据，看看各颗行星曾出现在天空的什么位置。当时有一位天文学家，第谷·布拉赫。他是个非常富有、行事古怪的
